result.markdown: --- title: "Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds" subtitle: "Brant test · cut-point-specific logistic models · partial proportional odds · alternatives · Lab 3" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 2: one odds ratio per predictor - Today: **is that single OR legitimate?** - By the end you can: - run and read the **Brant test** - **see** a violation with separate binary models - fit a **partial proportional-odds** model - decide what to do ::: # Topic 1 — Testing {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## The Brant test ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE) br <- brant(m2); round(br[, "probability"], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ---------------------------------------------------- Test for X2 df probability ---------------------------------------------------- Omnibus 58.74 20 0 wealth 1.11 2 0.57 educationPrimary 1.44 2 0.49 educationSecondary 1.68 2 0.43 educationHigher 2.74 2 0.25 bmi 0.64 2 0.72 anc_visits 1.33 2 0.52 parity 2.55 2 0.28 age 0.86 2 0.65 tribalYes 39.03 2 0 residenceRural 1.85 2 0.4 ---------------------------------------------------- H0: Parallel Regression Assumption holds ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Omnibus wealth educationPrimary educationSecondary 0.000 0.574 0.486 0.433 educationHigher bmi anc_visits parity 0.254 0.725 0.515 0.279 age tribalYes residenceRural 0.650 0.000 0.396 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the Brant test ::: {.incremental} - **Omnibus** test: do **any** predictors violate the assumption? - A p-value **per predictor**: here **tribal group** (p about 0); **wealth** (0.57), education, BMI and the others look fine - With many predictors, expect the occasional small p by chance; **look at the effect**, not only at p - It **warns** about sparse cells from continuous predictors: ignore the warning if the results are stable ::: ## See it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cuts <- c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe") or_for <- function(v) sapply(cuts, \(k) exp(coef(glm(I(as.numeric(mat$anaemia) >= which(levels(mat$anaemia) == k)) ~ wealth + tribal, family = binomial, data = mat))[v])) rbind(tribal = or_for("tribalYes"), wealth = or_for("wealth")) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mild.tribalYes Moderate.tribalYes Severe.tribalYes tribal 1.13 1.05 3.23 wealth 0.58 0.60 0.61 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Each column is a **separate binary logistic model**: "mild or worse", "moderate or worse", "severe". **Wealth's OR is the same in all three** (about 0.6): proportional odds holds. **Tribal's OR jumps to about 3 for severe anaemia only**: it does **not**. ::: # Topic 2 — What to do {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Partial proportional odds Free **only** the offending predictor (`ordinal::clm` with `nominal =`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_po <- ordinal::clm(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat) m_ppo <- ordinal::clm(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + residence, nominal = ~ tribal, data = mat) anova(m_po, m_ppo) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models: formula: m_po anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence m_ppo anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + residence nominal: link: threshold: m_po ~1 logit flexible m_ppo ~tribal logit flexible no.par AIC logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq) m_po 13 3134.6 -1554.3 m_ppo 15 3101.0 -1535.5 37.575 2 6.927e-09 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the comparison ::: {.incremental} - The likelihood-ratio test is **very small**: freeing tribal improves the fit a lot - All other predictors keep **one odds ratio each** - **Tribal gets a separate effect at each threshold** (for a worse category the OR is 1 / exp(coefficient): about 1.0, 0.9 and 2.8) ::: ## Options when the assumption fails | Option | Use when | |---|---| | **Partial proportional odds** | one or a few predictors violate it | | **Report cut-point-specific ORs** (separate binary models) | simple, transparent | | **Multinomial model** | many violations, or the order is doubtful | | **Keep the single OR** | mild violation, only a summary needed (say so) | | **Merge categories** | a sparse category drives it | ## Do not report one OR blindly ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(single_OR_tribal = round(exp(coef(m_po))[["tribalYes"]], 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` single_OR_tribal 1.11 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The single OR of about **1.1** averages "almost no effect on mild and moderate anaemia" with "a large effect on severe anaemia". Reporting it hides the finding that matters clinically. ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `ordinal-workshop/labs/lab3_po.R` - `brant()` omnibus and per predictor - binary models at each cut-point - `ordinal::clm()` with `nominal =` and a likelihood-ratio test ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtwbia.so757r" data-show="UHJvcG9ydGlvbmFsIG9kZHMgZmFpbHMgZm9yIHRyaWJhbCBncm91cCwgbm90IGZvciB3ZWFs dGg=" data-explain="VGhlIHRlc3QgaXMgcGVyIHByZWRpY3RvcjogYSBzbWFsbCBwIGZsYWdzIGEgcHJlZGljdG9y IHdob3NlIG9kZHMgcmF0aW8gZGlmZmVycyBhY3Jvc3MgY3V0LXBvaW50cy4gQSBsYXJnZSBw IGdpdmVzIG5vIGV2aWRlbmNlIGFnYWluc3QgdGhlIGFzc3VtcHRpb24gZm9yIHdlYWx0aC4="} The Brant test gives p < 0.001 for tribal group and p = 0.57 for wealth. What does this mean? - Tribal group has no effect while wealth has a very strong effect - Both predictors violate proportional odds, in different patterns - Proportional odds fails for tribal group, not for wealth - The model must be discarded for every one of the predictors in it ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtwoqy.so7jp3" data-show="VGhlIGVmZmVjdCB2YXJpZXMgYWNyb3NzIGN1dC1wb2ludHMsIHNvIHRoZSBhc3N1bXB0aW9u IGZhaWxz" data-explain="VW5kZXIgcHJvcG9ydGlvbmFsIG9kZHMgdGhlIHRocmVlIE9ScyB3b3VsZCBiZSBlcXVhbCBh cGFydCBmcm9tIGNoYW5jZS4gQSBqdW1wIGF0IHRoZSBoaWdoZXN0IGN1dC1wb2ludCBpcyBh IGNsZWFyIHZpb2xhdGlvbi4="} Separate binary models give tribal ORs of 1.1 (mild or worse), 1.0 (moderate or worse) and 3.2 (severe). What does this show? - The tribal effect is the same at each cut-point, so the model is right - The effect varies across cut-points, so the assumption fails - Severe anaemia was measured incorrectly in the tribal women studied - The sample of tribal women is too large for the test to be valid ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtx1zo.so7y6h" data-show="SXQgZnJlZXMgdGhlIHByb2JsZW0gcHJlZGljdG9yLCBrZWVwaW5nIG9uZSBPUiBmb3IgdGhl IHJlc3Q=" data-explain="SW4gY2xtLCBub21pbmFsID0gfiB4IGZyZWVzIHggb25seTsgdGhlIG90aGVyIHByZWRpY3Rv cnMga2VlcCBwcm9wb3J0aW9uYWwgZWZmZWN0cy4gVGhpcyBrZWVwcyB0aGUgZWZmaWNpZW5j eSBvZiB0aGUgb3JkaW5hbCBtb2RlbCB3aGVyZSBpdCBpcyB2YWxpZC4="} What does a partial proportional-odds model do? - It drops the problem predictor from the model that is being fitted - It converts the outcome into a binary variable for every woman - It frees the problem predictor, keeping one OR for the rest - It estimates a separate model for each woman in the data ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtxf8e.so8cnv" data-show="RnJlZWluZyBpdCBpbXByb3ZlcyB0aGUgZml0IGEgbG90OiB0aGUgYXNzdW1wdGlvbiBmYWls cw==" data-explain="VGhlIHByb3BvcnRpb25hbCBtb2RlbCBpcyBuZXN0ZWQgaW4gdGhlIHBhcnRpYWwgb25lOyBh IHNpZ25pZmljYW50IHRlc3QgbWVhbnMgdGhlIGV4dHJhIGZsZXhpYmlsaXR5IGlzIG5lZWRl ZC4="} A likelihood-ratio test comparing the proportional and the partial model has p < 0.001. What do you conclude? - The proportional-odds model fits better than the partial model does - The two models are identical, so either one may be reported - The predictor must be removed from both of the models being compared - Freeing it improves the fit a lot: the assumption fails ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtxsh0.so8r55" data-show="R2l2ZSBpdHMgT1IgYXQgZWFjaCBjdXQtcG9pbnQgYW5kIGV4cGxhaW4gdGhlIHBhdHRlcm4g c2Vlbg==" data-explain="VGhlIHBhdHRlcm4gYWNyb3NzIGN1dC1wb2ludHMgaXMgdGhlIGZpbmRpbmcuIEEgc2luZ2xl IE9SIHdvdWxkIGF2ZXJhZ2Ugb3ZlciB2ZXJ5IGRpZmZlcmVudCBlZmZlY3RzLg=="} Which is the best way to report a predictor that violates proportional odds? - Give its OR at each cut-point and explain the pattern seen - Report the single OR and stay silent about the violation found - Report only the p-value from the Brant test, with no estimate - Delete the predictor from the data so that the model fits again ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Brant test** per predictor + omnibus; **see** it with binary models at each cut - Partial proportional odds with `clm(nominal = ~ x)` - Alternatives: **cut-specific ORs**, **multinomial**, merge categories - Never report a **single OR** that hides a violation ::: **Next:** Session 4: multinomial logistic regression

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
